html:
The Battle of Bạch Đằng was fought in late 938 on the Bạch Đằng River near Hạ Long Bay in northern Vietnam. The Vietnamese leader Ngô Quyền destroyed the fleet of the Chinese state of Southern Han, ending about a thousand years of Chinese rule.

Chinese rule over the Red River delta had begun with the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE. When the Tang dynasty fell, local lords took control, and Southern Han, based in Guangzhou, sent a fleet under its prince Liu Hongcao to take the land back.

Ngô Quyền had large wooden stakes tipped with iron driven into the riverbed. At high tide, when the stakes were hidden, his small boats lured the Chinese fleet upriver. As the tide went out, the Chinese ships were caught on the stakes and destroyed, and Liu Hongcao was killed. In 939 Ngô Quyền made himself king. Vietnam remained independent for most of the next nine centuries; see Đại Việt. The same trick was used on the same river in 1288 by Trần Hưng Đạo against the Mongols.
